name: Cell Division and FtsZ Ring Assembly
description: Cell division in E. coli is initiated by assembly of the FtsZ ring (Z-ring) at the future division site (midcell). FtsZ is a tubulin-like GTPase that polymerizes into protofilaments which bundle to form a contractile ring structure. Z-ring placement is controlled by the Min system (oscillates pole-to-pole, inhibiting FtsZ at poles) and nucleoid occlusion (Noc/SlmA prevents division over unsegregated chromosomes). Once positioned, FtsZ recruits over 30 other divisome proteins in a hierarchical order: early arrivals (FtsA, ZipA stabilize Z-ring), middle arrivals (FtsK, FtsQ, FtsL, FtsB), and late arrivals (FtsW, FtsI for peptidoglycan synthesis). The coordinated action of these proteins drives septal peptidoglycan synthesis, membrane constriction, and cell separation. This flowchart illustrates the complete pathway from Z-ring assembly site selection through divisome maturation and cytokinesis.
scientificAccuracy: This flowchart is based on decades of genetic, cell biological, and structural studies of E. coli cell division. All divisome components (FtsZ, Min proteins, FtsA, ZipA, FtsK, FtsQLB, FtsWI, etc.), spatial regulation systems, and assembly hierarchy have been validated through genetics, microscopy, and recent super-resolution imaging. The model represents current understanding of how bacteria achieve accurate cell division with proper chromosome segregation.

notes: Cell division must be precisely coordinated with chromosome replication and segregation to ensure each daughter cell receives complete genetic information. The Min system oscillates with a ~20 second period, creating a time-averaged gradient that positions the Z-ring at midcell. FtsZ is conserved across bacteria and archaea and is homologous to tubulin, suggesting an ancient origin. The recent discovery that FtsW is the septal peptidoglycan synthase (not just a lipid II flippase) resolved a long-standing question about septal wall synthesis. Division is a major antibiotic target (β-lactams inhibit FtsI), and understanding divisome assembly may enable new antimicrobial strategies.
